title: Prompt Anatomy and Success Criteria
summary: After this intermediate-level module, you can turn an underspecified request into a structured prompt and define observable criteria for evaluating its output. You will also be able to diagnose whether a weak result is more likely related to missing context, unclear constraints, or absent success criteria.
objectives: Identify the task, context, constraints, output format, examples, and success criteria in a prompt.
Rewrite an underspecified request so that its required outcome and relevant context are explicit.
Define success criteria that can be checked against an output.
Diagnose common prompt problems by locating missing or conflicting components.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you can already write a basic text instruction and inspect the resulting output. It does not assume programming knowledge, familiarity with a named provider, or knowledge above the intermediate level.

Prompt anatomy is a practical way to examine the information inside a prompt. The labels used here are task, context, constraints, output format, examples, and success criteria. Not every prompt needs every component, but separating them makes omissions and conflicts easier to detect.

sections.title: Source correction
paragraphs: The previous citation was the local path content/modules/ai-foundations/prompt-anatomy-and-success-criteria.json. That source had an unregistered publisher, had never been verified, and was not a resolvable HTTPS reference.

This update replaces that citation with the canonical arXiv record for The Prompt Report: A Systematic Survey of Prompting Techniques. The change affects the source record and the support for the module's prompt terminology. The provider-neutral scope and the instructional focus on prompt components and checkable success criteria are unaffected.

sections.title: Components of a prompt
paragraphs: The task states the action to perform. A task such as “summarize this report” names an action, but it may still be underspecified if the intended reader, required coverage, or acceptable length is unknown.

Context supplies information needed to perform the task appropriately. It can identify the audience, purpose, background, definitions, or source material. Relevant context narrows plausible interpretations of the task.

Constraints set boundaries. They can limit length, exclude particular material, require the use of supplied evidence, or restrict the response to a defined scope. A constraint should be written so that a reviewer can determine whether it was followed.

The output format describes the expected organization or representation of the answer. Examples include a paragraph, a table with named columns, or a fixed sequence of fields. Format requirements should not conflict with one another.

Examples demonstrate a desired input-output relationship or a particular style of response. An example is most useful when it illustrates a requirement that would otherwise be difficult to express precisely.

Success criteria describe the properties an acceptable output must have. They differ from a general preference because they are observable. “Make it good” is not directly checkable, while “state the recommendation, give two reasons from the supplied text, and remain under 150 words” can be checked.

sections.title: From a request to a testable prompt
paragraphs: Begin by stating the task as a concrete action. Then add only the context needed to resolve meaningful ambiguity. Specify constraints and the output format separately so that each requirement is easy to inspect.

Next, convert preferences into success criteria. For each criterion, ask what evidence in the output would show that it was satisfied. If no reviewer could make that determination from the output and the supplied material, revise the criterion.

For example, the request “Write a useful summary” leaves usefulness undefined. A more testable prompt is: “Summarize the supplied policy for new employees. State its purpose, the three required actions, and the deadline. Use no more than 120 words, and do not add information that is absent from the policy.” The task is to summarize, the context identifies the audience and source, the constraints limit length and unsupported additions, and the success criteria identify required content.

After drafting, check for conflicts. A prompt that requires a complete explanation while also imposing a length too short to contain the required details has incompatible requirements. Resolve that conflict before evaluating the output.
sections.callout: A success criterion should let a reviewer point to evidence in the output or identify a specific missing requirement.

sections.title: Diagnosing results
paragraphs: When an output is weak, compare it with the prompt component by component. If the response addresses the wrong audience, relevant context may be missing. If it includes unwanted material, a scope constraint may be absent. If its organization varies between attempts, the output format may be underspecified.
If the output appears fluent but you cannot decide whether it is acceptable, the prompt probably lacks checkable success criteria. Add criteria before merely adding more descriptive language.

Do not assume that every failure can be corrected through wording alone. If the required information is absent from the supplied material, whether the task can be completed accurately is UNKNOWN. Supply the missing information or narrow the task rather than asking for unsupported content.

questions.prompt: Which requirement is a checkable success criterion?
choices: State the recommendation and give two reasons from the supplied text.
questions.explanation: The requirement to state a recommendation and give two reasons from the supplied text identifies evidence that a reviewer can check.

questions.prompt: A response is written for specialists, but the intended readers are new employees. Which prompt component most directly needs correction?
questions.explanation: The module explains that context can identify the audience. Stating that the readers are new employees helps resolve the audience mismatch.

questions.prompt: Which revision best turns “Write a useful summary” into a testable prompt?
choices: Write a useful and excellent summary.
Summarize the supplied policy for new employees, state its purpose and three required actions, and use no more than 120 words.
Summarize it however you think is best.
questions.explanation: This revision identifies the source and audience, specifies required content, and supplies a measurable length constraint.

questions.prompt: What should you do when accurate completion requires information that is absent from the supplied material?
choices: Request or supply the missing information, or narrow the task.
Treat the missing information as established fact.
questions.explanation: The module states that completion is UNKNOWN when required information is absent. The appropriate response is to provide that information or narrow the task.
